records.title: Show HN: The Zelda timeline to catch up before the Ocarina of Time remake
records.author: jsomau
records.storyText:
I made this ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake which comes out in 17 days. I remember the feeling of playing it as a kid but I hadn’t kept up with the story so I built a timeline to catch up before the Door of Time reopens.

Nintendo’s own timeline is the authority here (Hyrule Historia and their chronicle page). The fun part was rethinking how to visualize it. It branches at the end of Ocarina into three eras depending on whether Link wins or loses, so each era is its own thread on the cloth. The threads meet again much later with Breath of the Wild.

I had a lot of help from Claude. I’d often thought about building things like this but never found the time between the day job and the rest of life.

records.author: savydv
records.storyText:
I originally built ThemesFor.app in 2018 while running a small web development agency.

One thing that kept bothering me with website builders was that they increasingly tried to hide the technical parts of building a website. That's useful for many people, but I wanted almost the opposite — a visual tool for people who are already comfortable with HTML and CSS.

ThemesFor.app is my attempt at that.

You can build static websites from blocks, edit them visually, and export the HTML. I'm now working on taking the idea much further, but before I do, I wanted to put the current version in front of developers and see what they find useful—and what they don't.

It's still rough in places, so feedback is very welcome:

https://themesfor.app

records.title: Show HN: Cosplay as a tech lead, using gVisor to sandbox agents
records.author: SftwareRenderer
records.storyText:
Hi everyone,

This started as an exploration into harnesses and locally hostable LLMs (the kind that uses less power than a small electric heater), and I used it as an opportunity to retool. I've tried popular ones like Cline, Claude Code, and Pi, but wanted a different UX and integrated sandboxes.

The solution that I've landed on is a responsive web interface where I can quickly drive progress. It feels like a microcosm of my day job: define and delegate tasks, organize using kanban, then review deliverables. And it also feels like the time I used to spend coding is now spent in code review with the agent, so I tried to optimize the UX to make review feel nicer.

One of my (maybe a bit niche) benchmark use-cases is how pleasant it is to make progress on hobby software projects while also out on a hike. This meant specifying low bandwidth usage and offline mode.

Now I can jot down an idea, start the task, and at some point down the trail: get a notification* that either clarification is needed, a decision needs to be made, or the code is ready for review. I've been having a good time with this.

To build MIKE, I exclusively used locally hostable LLMs (from Google, Meta, Qwen, Poolside, and DeepSeek) hosted with llama.cpp on my machines at home (Strix Halo and a 5090) to "compile" the code. The experience has gotten substantially better ever since DeepSeek’s release in July. Side note: I have a soft spot for llama.cpp since it was one of the first that made it possible to run this new tech at home, and its maintainers accepted a tiny improvement I made to error reporting. Oh the joys of having a PR get approved.

I plan on maintaining this, at least until similar features are supported by better tools. Until then, hope you find this useful!

5 minute demo: https://youtu.be/jexzLkZ50FU

p.s.

I didn't mention details about the sandbox earlier since most people seem to find this a bit boring. It was one of my critical requirements, and I opted to use an existing battle-tested sandbox. I'm not an expert on how the Linux kernel works, but seeing all the VM escape exploits recently is a bit scary, and I liked gVisor’s approach to the problem.

I'm also using Git worktrees to provision the agent’s workspace, as well as a read-only repository mount to provide relevant context when the agent looks for it.

*off by default

records.title: Show HN: BricksChat – Generate Lego builds from images, including Technic
records.author: mireklzicar
records.storyText:
I've been working on generative LEGO assembly models recently, but there are similar projects already, so I wanted to try some harder cases: specialized parts (incl. technic), multi-modal prompting (incl. using images, 3D meshes or almost any input), constrained inventory (so you could upload just parts you have), ensuring physical validity and generating buildable instructions, being able to tweak, modify or rebuild entirely an existing build etc.

TL;DR the pipeline got more complex than expected and I ended up with an agentic harness leveraging recursive program synthesis, combinatorial diffusion, semantic 3D search and operations on assembly hypergraphs.

Yet I am quite happy with the result. It should be able to handle as well a functional mechanism, LEGO robot, artistic landscape or fancy animal.

Most importantly, it also checks for subgraph matches of builds present in catalogue, being able to check (and possibly enforce) originality and prevent copying existing MOCs.

Have fun!

records.title: Show HN: Connecting Captions Local Private AI Interpreter
records.author: chrisswimlee
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I built Connecting Captions, a live captioning and translation overlay for macOS that runs entirely on-device. Nothing goes over the network: no API calls, no audio leaving your machine, and it keeps working offline.

I wanted live translation I could use in meetings and conversations without worrying about connectivity, latency spikes, or sending sensitive audio to a third party.

The technically interesting part is a low-latency, self-correcting pipeline for speech-to-text and translation. It has two modes:

Sentence mode: buffers until a sentence boundary, then translates with full context. It’s more accurate, especially between languages with different word order. Streaming mode: translates word by word as speech arrives, trading grammatical accuracy for minimal delay.

Current state:

Platform: macOS Models: Whisper Latency: ~200 ms Languages: 25

Code: https://github.com/chrisswimlee/connectingCaptions

I’d love feedback, especially on the self-correction approach and which use cases matter most to people.

records.title: Show HN: Risphai – picks the AI model, tools and prompt for each request
records.author: risphere
records.storyText:
I noticed that a lot of non-technical people don’t use AI to its full extent. Like they use the wrong model for the task, the wrong reasoning effort, or vague prompts. That gap between "what the AI can do" and "what people actually get" is what I wanted to fix.

So I spent the last two years in my spare time building a consumer AI product that tries to fix this issue.

This is how it works: When it receives the request, an LLM decides the task type (chat, reasoning, coding, writing) and the tool calls that are needed (web search, image generation, video generation, audio generation). Then it routes it to a suitable model and applies a prompt based on the task type. If it's a media generation task, it rewrites the prompt into a detailed one using prompt formulas (the prompt formulas for specific styles are mentioned in the system prompt). The LLM that is used for answering the request can also use a map, generate a mermaid diagram, generate a quiz or flashcards, generate files, etc.

A limitation right now is that routing adds latency, but I'm currently experimenting with decision-models like Jev, PPLX Decider, etc. and might use decision-models to route to the right LLM and give the tool calls like web search and media generation to the answering LLM.

It launched this week, so it's still early and I will keep improving it and adding new things.

Also sign-up/in is required to prevent abuse.

I’d really like honest feedback: what’s confusing, what’s missing, etc.

records.storyText:
About a year ago I was wondering how hard it'd be to build an e2e enabled emacs matrix client similar to how telega does things: use mature libraries to build a daemon that speaks JSON to emacs.

I did a proof of concept for the e2e bits, and over time built a chat client on top. I recently switched to it as my only client on most devices - and thought maybe it's time to give it a better name than "matrix", and cut it out of my .emacs.d it was developed in. So I asked an LLM to write tests for everything to have a sensible baseline, split it out, and renamed everything.

There probably is still a bit of breakage linking back to my config, but I'm relatively confident all major issues got fixed over the last week of testing.

Here you have 13 different rocket engine technologies, 9 have flown, 3 built and test fired, but not flown and 1 never completed.

I created this site because I wanted to learn more about rocket engines and how they work. My background is HVAC/plumbing engineer and 3D artist, not rocket engineer, so I built this just out of my personal curiosity.

Here you can investigate each motor type and learn what each part does, explode and cutaway the model and see how fuel and oxidizer flow to generate the thrust.

Site is created using Claude Opus 5.5. Claude made also the 3D models using Blender MCP. Site runs on Babylon.js 9.16.1 on WebGL2.

What I did was basically art direction and fact checking. It took me about one week, among other projects, to get this site finalized so that I was happy about the design and outcome.

Any improvements, corrections and comments are welcome!

records.title: Show HN: Parents Inbox – Communication Guide for Schools
records.author: sxates
records.storyText:
At a dinner party with other parents recently, the conversation turned to the challenges we all have with communication coming from our children's schools. Emails and Texts and App notifications, coming from Teachers, Admins, PTA, After-Care programs. Overlapping information, buried key details, verbose fluff. An avalanche of text every day that must be carefully parsed to find important info.

This seems to be a universal problem and certainly one I experience every day. So literally before dinner was over I built the first version of this site on my phone with Claude.

I think the main problem is that the folks who are responsible for communication just don't have the tools and experience to know what good communication really looks like, or the parents perspective hasn't been demonstrated to them to give them more empathy. So I am hoping this can help. Feel free to share if you have the same problem with your school.
